job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Aaron Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aaron. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee auditor at Hartley and Pryce, a mid-size firm in Birmingham. Most days I sit with a client's ledgers, tick sales invoices against bank statements and write up what I found in a working paper. I share a flat in Selly Oak with two mates from uni and get the bus in at half eight. I like the ticking, honestly. It's slow and exact and nobody rushes me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, we keep doing audits properly. To my mates I'd say the hype is a sales pitch from people who sell software. Online I'd probably say nothing, I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record I'm relieved, because I like my job as it is. Dev (my senior) keeps showing us a sampling tool the firm bought, and I tick by hand beside it. If it stays a small helper I can carry on without it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, really. I'd keep studying for my chartered accountancy exams, which the firm pays for, and keep paying into the union I joined at uni. Over the first year I'd save about four hundred a month from my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even a bit smug, if I'm honest. My parents told me accounting is a safe trade and this picture says they're right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you avoid the sampling tool. What happens when a manager asks why you're slower than the others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It did happen in September. My manager Priti said I was a day behind on a retail client, and I told her my sample was cleaner. It was, I found a missed invoice the tool had skipped. She let it go, but a day behind adds up in busy season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which worry would you still carry even if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, mainly. It's five hundred and fifty a month for my room and it keeps creeping up. My parents say they'll help if I ask, so it's pride more than panic. I also worry the firm gets bought by a bigger one, which happens a lot.

say: I'd tell colleagues that **audits** carry on as they are and the hype is a software sales pitch.
I'd tell my mates the loudest voices are the people selling the tools.
think: I'm quietly **relieved**, because I like ticking and tying by hand and don't want to change how I work.
The firm's sampling tool stays a side show, so I can keep ignoring it.
do: Keep studying for the **chartered exams** the firm pays for.
Stay in the union and save about **£400 a month** from my pay.
feel: **Calm**, and a little smug that my parents' advice on a safe trade is holding up.
S0.quote: Even a bit smug, if I'm honest. My parents told me accounting is a safe trade and this picture says they're right.
fieldNote: Likes **slow, exact work** and sees the tool as a rival rather than help.
Strong **cushion** and parents' backing explain the calm; the manager's remark about speed is his one soft spot.
Pride, more than money, would stop him asking for help.

steps.text: Keep studying for the chartered accountancy exams the firm pays for
Save about 400 pounds a month towards a flat deposit
Stay in the union and attend its monthly meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. It's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the firm should talk to staff before moving tasks to software. To my mates I'd say juniors like me are the ones who pay for it. Online I'd back the audit union's campaign for a say in new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I know ticking and tying is the first thing they'd hand to the tool. Dev says it already does about a third of my sample testing on one client. If I refuse to learn it, I'm the slowest person doing what it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally sit with Dev for a week and learn the tool, but only so I can check its work. I'd push the union rep to ask for a rule that the firm tells us before any task is moved. And I'd book the next exam sitting early, so I'm qualified before the next intake is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a little. I've got money and my parents behind me, so it isn't dread. It's more that the thing I'm good at is losing value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tool. That's a change from today. What makes it different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it would be a job question, not a taste question. Right now I can say my way is more careful and get away with it. When the firm hires two juniors fewer, careful isn't an argument any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if the firm shrinks its junior team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the tool, and not really Priti. The partners who see a salary line they can delete, and ministers who let firms mark their own homework. Rules on who must sign off an audit are what protect juniors, and I'd want them kept.

say: I'd ask the firm to **talk to staff** before it moves any task to software.
I'd say juniors pay first, and back the union's push for a **say in new tools**.
think: Ticking and tying is the first thing handed to the tool, so my own **tasks** are the ones at risk.
If I stay the slowest at what the tool does, I become the easy cut.
do: Spend a week with Dev learning the tool, only to **check its work**.
Ask the union rep for a rule that staff are told **before tasks move**.
Book the next exam sitting early to qualify sooner.
feel: **Anxious** but not scared, because savings and my parents cushion me; the worry is my skill losing value.
S1.quote: When the firm hires two juniors fewer, careful isn't an argument any more.
fieldNote: First time he agrees to **change**, and only because the argument for staying careful stops working.
Blames **partners** and weak regulation, not the software or his manager.
Anxious about value of his skill, not about money.

steps.text: Spend a week with Dev learning the sampling tool
Ask the union rep for a rule that staff are told before tasks move
Book the next chartered exam sitting early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a plan from the partners within the month. To friends I'd say this is what regulation is for, and it's late. Online I'd be loud about it, which I'm not normally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? Two years is shorter than my training contract. I'd qualify the same month the work I qualified to do is done by software. I'd be the person who spent years learning to tick things by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every spare pound into savings, about eight hundred a month from now. I'd join the union's political campaign and email my MP about a transition fund. And I'd learn the AI tools, late and unwillingly, because being the one who can't is worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd sleep badly. My mum would tell me to stay calm and I'd snap at her, which I hate doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would two years feel so different from five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can't retrain in two years and keep my head above water. Qualifying takes three and a half. With longer, I can learn another profession alongside. With two, I'm choosing blind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad, who's a rail union rep, that we need what his lot fought for in the nineties, but for office work. I'd ask them to keep the flat deposit fund they set aside for me ready. I'd feel like a child asking, and I'd ask anyway.

say: I'd demand the partners give staff a **plan within a month**.
I'd say this is what regulation exists for, and I'd be loud online.
think: Two years is shorter than my **training contract**, so I'd qualify into work already gone.
I can't retrain in time and I'd be choosing **blind**.
do: Put every spare pound into savings, about **£800 a month**.
Join the union's political campaign and email my MP about a **transition fund**.
Learn the AI tools, late and unwillingly.
feel: **Alarmed**; I'd sleep badly and snap at my mum, which I hate.
S2.quote: Two years is shorter than my training contract.
fieldNote: Stops resisting **tools** only when the clock leaves no choice.
Family money and a **deposit fund** soften the fall but he is ashamed to ask.
Treats the timeline as the whole problem.

steps.text: Save about 800 pounds a month from now
Email my MP asking for a retraining and transition fund
Learn the firm's AI tools well enough to check them
Ask my parents to keep the flat deposit fund ready

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is enough to rebuild how we train juniors, if the firm starts now. To friends I'd say the unions and the government should be negotiating today. Online I'd share the union's reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think my first five years in the job are when the ladder gets cut under me. Seniors survive because clients know them. Juniors get replaced because nobody notices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd learn the tools properly with Dev and take a bigger share of client meetings so people know me. I'd stay with the exams. And I'd aim to have a year of rent in the bank before 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. Five years feels like a stretch of road where I can still steer. My parents' help makes it bearable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I get to change on purpose rather than in a panic. In two years I'd freeze. In five I can learn the tool, move towards advising clients and still have a normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You avoid new technology today. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't, fully. I know I'm slow to start, but I do start once I'm convinced. The union helps, because it gives me a group to learn with, and I'd rather do that than learn alone.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **rebuild junior training** if the firm starts now.
I'd tell friends unions and government should be **negotiating today**.
think: The ladder gets cut under **juniors** first, because clients know seniors but nobody notices a junior leaving.
I need people to know my name before then.
do: Learn the tools properly with Dev and take more **client meetings**.
Build **a year of rent** in the bank within about three years.
feel: **Anxious but steady**, because five years still lets me steer.
S3.quote: Seniors survive because clients know them. Juniors get replaced because nobody notices.
fieldNote: Longer **warning** turns panic into a plan: be known by clients and learn the tools in a group.
Admits he is **slow to start** but does start once convinced.
Relies on the union as a way to learn, not only to protest.

steps.text: Learn the audit tool properly with Dev over this winter
Take on more client meetings so clients know me
Keep sitting the chartered exams on schedule
Build a year of rent in savings by 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one, called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is long enough for the profession to rebuild itself. To friends I'd say this is the moment to argue for shorter weeks and a share of the gains. Online I'd stay quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel I'm fine for a long time. I'd be thirty-two. I'd have been qualified for years, and maybe I'd be a manager checking what the machines produce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my career, finish my exams and use the years to learn the tools slowly, one task at a time. I'd put money into a pension and a flat deposit. And I'd stay in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. It's a distant weather forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in year one if you knew it was ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop treating the tool as the enemy and treat it as a colleague I don't like. I'd also save for a deposit sooner, since a long timeline lets me plan a normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's generation, mostly, and small firms that can't afford the tools. If the gains only go to the big firms, that's the world I'd argue against.

say: I'd say ten years is long enough for the profession to **rebuild itself**.
I'd argue for **shorter weeks** and a share of the gains, mostly in private.
think: I'd be thirty-two and long qualified, maybe a **manager checking** what machines produce.
I feel fine for a long time.
do: Learn the tools slowly, **one task** at a time.
Pay into a pension and a flat **deposit fund**.
feel: **Uneasy**, not scared, like a distant weather forecast.
S4.quote: Uneasy, not scared. It's a distant weather forecast.
fieldNote: With **ten years** he softens, and calls the tool a colleague he doesn't like.
Worries for his **father's generation** and small firms more than himself.
Keeps his politics about who gets the gains.

steps.text: Learn one audit-tool task at a time over several years
Pay into a pension and a flat deposit fund
Stay in the union and push for shared gains

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, with two years. I can't retrain and qualify in that time, and I'd be stuck with a skill nobody wants. A fund for retraining and a rule that firms tell staff before moving tasks to software would help. I'd also want an office workers' union with real weight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as anti-technology as I sound. I'm not against the machine. I'm against it landing on juniors before anyone asks us.

headlineQuote: I'm not against the machine. I'm against it landing on juniors before anyone asks us.
portrait: Aaron is a **22-year-old trainee auditor** in Birmingham, top of his class, with no debt and family backing.
He likes slow, exact work and **avoids AI tools**, treating the firm's sampling tool as a rival.
He blames **partners and weak regulation**, not software, and puts faith in his union.
He stays calm when nothing changes, then turns **anxious or alarmed** as the warning time shrinks.
He learns the tools only when the argument for staying careful stops working.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most, because two years is too short to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining fund** and a rule that firms tell staff before moving tasks to software.
An **office workers' union** with real weight.
